summary: Summarizes the TLV codepoints in use by the IS-IS routing protocol and its pending extensions, as used by several ISPs. It records which numbers are taken so that new extensions do not collide with them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3359 is a reference list for IS-IS, a routing protocol. IS-IS messages carry pieces of information, and each piece has a number tag saying what it is. The memo collects all the tags in use so that people adding new features do not accidentally reuse a number.

questions: what tlv codepoints does is-is use
where are is-is tlv numbers listed
which is-is tlv codes are reserved
subtitle: A shared list of which type numbers IS-IS already uses, kept so new extensions do not collide.

tldr.problem: IS-IS carries information in Type, Length and Value blocks, and no central authority hands out the type numbers, so independent extensions could choose the same number.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists every TLV codepoint in use at the time, with its number, the packet types it may appear in and where it is defined.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and explicitly not an authority; it says it may be replaced at any time by some type of official registry.

today: RFC 3359 is Informational, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The text itself says it may be replaced at any time by some type of official registry.

sections.title: Why a List of Codepoints
sections.content:
IS-IS is an interior gateway routing protocol, developed originally by OSI and used with IP extensions as an Interior Gateway Protocol. Its messages carry information in TLV blocks, each with a type, a length and a value. The memo describes codepoints used by several ISPs for routing within their clouds, and it includes the protocol's pending extensions.

The purpose is to avoid future conflicts in assigning TLV numbers. The core IS-IS protocol is specified in the ISO standards body, while IP extensions to it are products of the IETF IS-IS working group. Because ISO provides no numbering authority and IANA is responsible only for IP-related coding points, the memo says no plausible central authority to assign TLV numbers exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Many people add new kinds of information to the same message format. A shared list of numbers keeps two people from using one number for two different things.

sections.title: The Reserved TLV Table
sections.content:
The table lists one row per TLV: its name, its value, whether it may appear in IIH (hello), LSP (link state) and SNP (sequence number) packets, and its status. The status column names the source, such as ISO 10589, RFC 1195, RFC 2763 or an IETF-draft.

Examples include Area Addresses (1), Padding (8), Authentication (10), IP Int. Reach (128), Protocols Supported (129), Dynamic Name (137), IPv6 Intf. Addr. (232) and P2P Adjacency State (240). Two entries are vendor proprietary (Lucent 66, and Nortel 176 and 177), and DECnet Phase IV (42) is labelled ancient. Code 133 is marked Illegal and not used.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is a chart: each tag has a number, a name, which kinds of messages may carry it, and who defined it.

sections.title: Assignment Procedures and Security
sections.content:
The document does not constitute or represent any standard or authority assigning TLV numbers. Assignment happens on a shared, informational basis between ISO, SIF and the IETF working groups. The memo is to be updated periodically in the fashion of the Assigned Numbers practice, and it may be replaced at any point by some type of official registry. It does not indicate which documents use the codepoints, and it does not resolve sub-TLV codepoints.

On security, the RFC says IS-IS security applies to the work presented and no specific security issues are being introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is a helpful notice board, not a rulebook or an authority. A real official registry might replace it one day.

references.text: Reynolds, J., "Assigned Numbers; RFC 1700 is Replaced by an On-line Database", RFC 3232, January 2002.
